title: Anandpur Sahib
hookLine: the city of bliss, the Khalsa's birthplace

cards: A town's name can be a promise. This one is Anandpur, the city of bliss, tucked against low green hills in Punjab.
At Hola Mohalla it fills up: drums, horses kicking up dust, blue and saffron banners, riders showing off old skills in an open field, and kitchens feeding everyone who comes.
Sikhs remember it as the place where the Khalsa was born. And in Sikh memory it also knew sieges and hunger. A city of bliss, and a city of hard days.
How can both be true of one place?

teach.b: Start with how it began. Tradition says Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, founded the town in the hills, and it became the home of his son, Guru Gobind Singh. Then its great day.
Sikhs remember that here, at a Vaisakhi gathering, Guru Gobind Singh asked who would give their head, and from those who stood up he formed the Khalsa, the Guru's own.
Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib stands where tradition places that day, one of the Takhts, the seats of Sikh authority. Then the hard part. Anandpur didn't stay peaceful.
Tradition remembers armies around the town, hunger inside it, and the night the Guru's household left and was scattered on the road. Tomorrow's place belongs to that road. So why call it bliss?

The Anand Sahib is a hymn of Guru Amar Das, the third Guru, and Sikhs sing it at weddings and other gatherings. It opens, in paraphrase, with a voice telling its mother: I am in bliss, because I have found the True Guru.
The bliss in the hymn isn't a calm afternoon or a good harvest. It comes from meeting the Guru.
Anand is not the absence of trouble; it is the Guru's presence.

That's how a town that knew sieges can carry the name city of bliss without any irony. Today Anandpur Sahib is a town of gurdwaras, quiet most days and packed at Hola Mohalla. The hills behind it are the same hills.

how: Sikhs visit Anandpur Sahib all year, especially Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib, and gather there in large numbers for Hola Mohalla, with kirtan, langar and displays of martial skill.

games.why: the hymn opens with a voice telling its mother: I am in bliss, because I have found the True Guru.

practice: See a ring of low green hills, a river below, a town at their feet. Let the town get loud, drums, horses, kitchens smoking, and then let it go quiet, one lamp in a window, while the hills stay steady behind it all.
If you pray, rest with the opening of the Anand Sahib; if not, just rest with the hills.

wordCard.voice: Anandpur Sahib. The city of bliss in the hills of Punjab, where Sikhs remember the Khalsa was born, and where Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib stands. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: anand, bliss, with pur, town. the city of bliss.

carryVoice: Your line: city of bliss. Joy can live in a place that has known hard days. I'll be here tomorrow.
